reference_title: EM 1110-1-1905, Geotechnical Design of Shallow Foundations on Soils (USACE, 31 July 2025)

sections.title: Introduction
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-1, printed p. 233.

sections.title: Problematic ground conditions are those which do not fit conventional theories …
sections.body: [p. 233] Problematic ground conditions are those which do not fit conventional theories of soil and rock mechanics or that generally require avoidance or extensive mitigation for shallow foundation support. Such characteristics are often attributable to their composition or behavior, which can be inconsistent or unreliable. Common problematic ground conditions and their characteristics are discussed in this chapter.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-1a, printed p. 233. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Common problematic ground conditions are summarized in Table 10-1
sections.body:
[p. 233] Common problematic ground conditions are summarized in Table 10-1. Where encountered or suspected, geohazards (problematic ground) should be identified and documented during site exploration activities and the expected behavior addressed during foundation design. For problematic ground sites, soil behavior can be difficult to predict, and therefore, more qualitative assessments may be necessary. Often, the potential for unsatisfactory performance (and associated risk) cannot be eliminated.

Table 10-1 Some common problem ground conditions
Condition | Potential Engineering Challenges
Uncontrolled and undocumented fill | Could be inconsistent or unreliable. Could incorporate environmental contaminants. Extent can be difficult to evaluate.
Expansive soils | Often expand (heave) upon wetting and shrink upon drying. Can result in unacceptable foundation movements. Limiting extreme soil moisture changes could be difficult. Difficult to avoid in some geographic regions.
Collapsible soils | Could undergo large, sudden, irrecoverable collapse and significant loss of shear strength that is primarily wetting-induced. Difficult to avoid in some geographic regions.
Colluvium or colluvial soils | Can be highly variable with a loose soil matrix. Nearby global stability could be a major issue with proposed structure. Geotechnical investigations often hindered by variable-sized rock content.
Karst | Soil erosion into complex underground solution features is difficult to predict and nearly impractical to avoid in certain geographic regions. Site grading can aggravate natural solutioning processes. Could result in extreme soil movements and collapse of foundation-supporting soils.
Frozen ground | Complex engineering behavior aggravated by temperature fluctuations and heat transfer from structures which could result in extreme movements. Impractical to avoid in some geographic regions.
Scour and erosion | Hydraulic conditions can be complex and unreliable. Loss of bearing soils could result in excessive movement or structure collapse.

sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-1b, printed p. 233. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Uncontrolled and undocumented fill
sections.body: [p. 234] Uncontrolled fills are materials placed by humans without engineering design and inspection. Undocumented fill could be either uncontrolled fill or otherwise acceptable fill; however, in some cases, a distinction cannot be easily made between the two because it was never documented, or documentation cannot be readily located.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-2, printed p. 234.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.body: [p. 234] Characteristics. Uncontrolled fills often contain soft or loose zones, trees, cobbles, boulders, cinders, or other construction or demolition debris. The consistency (or relative density) and moisture content of uncontrolled fill often varies significantly and within short distances. There is no practical amount of exploration or testing that can distinguish with certainty if an undocumented fill was placed in a controlled manner. In some cases, what may appear to be a controlled fill may include buried trees or other unsuitable material in unexplored areas. Often, uncontrolled fills are placed on unprepared and unsuitable subgrades containing large roots and organics, which aid in identification of uncontrolled fills.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-2a, printed p. 234.

sections.title: Performance issues
sections.body: [p. 234] Performance issues. Performance of uncontrolled fill is difficult to properly ascertain and quantify due to the possibility of large variations. Shallow foundations placed over uncontrolled fill could result in excessive settlement or collapse. According to Goodger and Leach (1991), the percentage of within-fill settlement (as a percentage of fill height alone) can exceed 3.5 percent for uncompacted sand, 12.0 percent for clay fill (pumped), and 30 percent for well-compacted mixed refuse. When placed over poor subgrades, additional long-term settlements could also occur in the underlying earth. If the uncontrolled fill incorporates hazardous waste or other environmental contaminants, disposal costs could be significant. Also, personnel exposure could result in sickness or death. Although it is possible to improve some uncontrolled fills, the possibility of unsatisfactory performance cannot be eliminated since certain unknown conditions will remain.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-2b, printed p. 234.

sections.title: Mitigation techniques
sections.body: [p. 234] Mitigation techniques. Uncontrolled fills are typically mitigated by avoidance, extending footings to competent strata, or removal and replacement with suitable earth fill. In some instances, ground improvement techniques (such as dynamic compaction, aggregate piers) have been implemented in efforts to mitigate potential performance issues associated with uncontrolled fill; however, the degree of improvement can be difficult to quantify.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-2c, printed p. 234.

sections.title: Expansive soils
sections.body: [p. 234] Expansive soils are those which swell considerably on absorption of water and shrink upon drying. Expansive or swelling soils are found in many areas throughout the United States (see Figure 10-1) and the world and pose the greatest hazard in regions with pronounced wet and dry seasons.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-3, printed p. 234.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.body: [p. 234] Characteristics. Expansive soils often consist of plastic clays and clay shales that typically contain colloidal clay minerals (that expand upon wetting) such as the montmorillonites or smectite. They include marls, clayey siltstone, sandstone, and [p. 235] saprolites. Some soils (such as dry, residual, clayey soil) may heave on wetting under low applied pressure but collapse at higher pressure. Other clayey soil may initially collapse on wetting, but heave over long periods of time as water slowly wets the less pervious clay particles. Desiccation can cause expansive soils to shrink. Additional engineering aspects such as site studies, identification, heave predictions, and foundation types are discussed in UFC 3-220-07.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-3a, printed pp. 234 to 235.

sections.title: Performance issues
sections.body: [p. 235] Performance issues. Excessive movements (both heave and swell) can cause damages to structures that are not adequately designed and managed to accommodate soil volume changes. Of primary concern are vertical soil movements since they can cause the most damage to overlying structures. Damage can include impaired function, cracked walls, and jammed and misaligned doors and windows. Important factors that contribute to damages are: (1) the failure to recognize the presence of expansive soil, (2) failure to implement reasonable mitigation measures, and (3) failure to manage soil moisture in the vicinity of the structure in an appropriate manner.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-3b, printed p. 235.

sections.title: Mitigation techniques
sections.body:
[p. 235] Mitigation techniques. Foundations are commonly placed below zones of high volume change due to moisture fluctuations. Physicochemical stabilizers (such as lime, cement, fly ash), by-product stabilizers (such as ground blast furnace slag, kiln dust) can also be used to mitigate expansive soils. Other methods include moisture conditioning/compaction control, drainage/soil moisture control, pre-wetting, and removal and replacement with soil having low volume change characteristics. Refer to UFC 3-220-07 for mitigation techniques.

[p. 236] Figure 10-1. Swelling clays map of the conterminous United States (USGS, Map I-1940 1989)

sections.title: Collapsible soils
sections.body:
[p. 236] Collapsible soils are unsaturated soils (typically silty sands with a loose structure) that undergo particle rearrangement upon wetting and additional loading (or both) and a significant decrease in volume. The primary triggering mechanism for volume reduction is an increase in moisture content, and collapse settlement cannot occur in soils below the water table. Numerous soil types can fall in the general category of collapsible soils as shown in Figure 10-2.

[p. 237] Figure 10-2. A family of collapsible soils (Rogers 1995)
figures: Figure 10-2: A family of collapsible soils (Rogers 1995)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-4, printed pp. 236 to 237.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.body: [p. 237] Characteristics. Collapsible soils are generally characterized as having a relatively low dry-unit weight, high void ratio, and a low saturation percentage (usually between 13 and 39). However, the identification and prediction of soil collapse has proven difficult because no single criterion can be applied to all collapsible soils. Collapsible soils can be found in debris-flow deposits in young alluvial fans, aeolian deposits such as dunes and loess, lacustrine and colluvial deposits, residual soils and tuff, loose sand and gravels, dispersive clays, and fills compacted dry of optimum content (Owens and Rollins 1990; Mulvey 1992; and Santi 2005).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-4a, printed p. 237.

sections.title: Performance issues
sections.body: [p. 237] Performance issues. Collapsible soils are problematic for shallow foundation support due to the capacity to undergo large, sudden, and irrecoverable collapse and significant loss of shear strength that is primarily wetting induced. Collapsible soils can also be susceptible to liquefaction-induced settlements during earthquakes, and wetting under load has proven ineffective at reducing liquefaction potential. Reliance on laboratory classification and consolidation tests alone can fail to indicate soil that eventually could collapse in the field. In some geologic settings, avoidance of collapsible soils is not practical.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-4b, printed p. 237.

sections.title: Mitigation techniques
sections.body: [p. 237] Mitigation techniques. Collapse potential can be assessed using ASTM D5333. If the collapsible soil layer is relatively thin and surficial, then removal and replacement with suitable soil or embedding foundations beneath is often preferred. Other alternatives include avoidance, pre-wetting (hydrocompaction) or controlled wetting to depths as great as 10 ft, avoidance of wetting, dynamic compaction, chemical stabilization or grouting, and differential-settlement-resistant foundations (such as continuous footing design with load-bearing beams).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-4c, printed p. 237.

sections.title: Colluvium or colluvial materials
sections.body: [p. 237] Colluvium is a general term that refers to loose, unconsolidated material that has been deposited by gravitational forces (especially those mobilized via mass wasting), usually collected at the base of gentle slopes or hillsides.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-5, printed p. 237.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.body: [p. 238] Characteristics. The characteristics of colluvial materials vary according to the characteristics of the parent material and the climate under which weathering and transport occur. Typically, colluvium is weakly stratified and consists of a heterogeneous mixture of soil and rock fragments ranging in size from clay particles to rocks that are several feet or more in diameter. In some cases, colluvium is not easily distinguished from alluvium (such as at the base of slopes and near alluvial deposits). Colluvium can accumulate slowly or result from large catastrophic earth movements (such as landslides) often attributed to intense rainfall, fire, or seismic activity. Subsurface drilling in colluvial soils is often difficult and test trenches can often provide better characterization than can be solely achieved with conventional drilling methods.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-5a, printed p. 238.

sections.title: Performance issues
sections.body: [p. 238] Performance issues. Placement of foundations on or near very loose and marginally stable colluvium could result in excessive movements. These movements could be due to settlement or instability of the colluvium itself, or due to adjacent slope movements (such as landslides). In some areas, landslides formed in colluvium are common and destructive. Commonly found along the lower portion of valley sides, they often need excavation for construction of structures, which could result in a more unstable configuration.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-5b, printed p. 238.

sections.title: Mitigation techniques
sections.body: [p. 238] Mitigation techniques. Colluvial deposits and planned modifications (such as cut/fill) of these deposits should be carefully evaluated for slope stability, recognizing that the deposits often have highly variable characteristics. Mitigation techniques usually include avoidance or removal and replacement. Often, buttress slopes or earth retention near unstable slopes are also necessary to prevent further instability.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-5c, printed p. 238.

sections.title: Organic soils and peat
sections.body: [p. 238] Organic soils are formed by the accumulation of partially decomposed organic matter and are most common in water-saturated, humid environments such as low-lying areas or swamps. Organic materials contain large pore spaces in their cellular structures and can hold significant water (Terzaghi and Peck 1967). This higher water content typically results in lower shear strength and higher compressibility. For engineering classification, organic soils and peat are unique materials having more complex definition compared to other inorganic soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-6, printed p. 238.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.body:
[p. 238] Characteristics. Organic soils and peat are generally characterized in Table 10-2a and Table 10-2b and may be qualitatively identified using the methods outlined in ASTM D2487/D2488. The amount of organic matter can be quantified by using a muffle furnace (ASTM D2974); however, some clay minerals contain bound water that could falsely indicate organic content (Arman and Munfakh 1970; Franklin et al. 1973). Engineering behavior is generally described in Table 10-3 (Edil and den Haan 1994).

sections.title: Performance issues
sections.body: [p. 240] Performance issues. Generally, soils containing large amounts of organic material (especially when greater than 5 percent) often exhibit poor engineering characteristics (such as high compressibility, low shear strength) and should not be used for shallow foundation support.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-6b, printed p. 240.

sections.title: Mitigation techniques
sections.body: [p. 241] Mitigation techniques. If unsuitable organic soils are present at foundation bearing elevations, mitigation measures typically include removal and replacement with suitably compacted, engineered fill. In areas where removal and replacement are not a viable option (such as organic soils exist to great depths), preloading, surcharging, and staged construction could result in effective ground improvement. Due to the loss of surface hydration water in clayey soils at very high temperatures, ASTM D2974 can be used in conjunction with other qualitative identification methods (such as ASTM D2487/D2488) or laboratory testing to prevent mischaracterization and an over- or under-conservative design.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-6c, printed p. 241.

sections.title: Karst terrain
sections.body: [p. 241] Karst landforms constitute approximately 12 percent of the ice-free land surface and result from mildly acidic water acting on carbonate (such as limestone, dolostone) and sulfate (such as gypsum) rocks. The (carbonic) acid is formed as rain passes through the atmosphere and, over geologic time, dissolves the bedrock surface, enlarges fractures, and results in underground voids and drainage systems. Reference also EM 1110-1-2908.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-7, printed p. 241.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.body: [p. 241] Characteristics. Karst landscapes exhibit an irregular topography characterized by streamless valleys, sinkholes, and streams that disappear underground, all developed by the action of groundwater (Leet et al. 1978). Depressions, gullies, caves, underground drainage, and sinkholes are commonly found in karst terrain. Rock dissolution occurs primarily from the surface downward and along the surfaces of fissures (such as joints, bedding planes, and fractures) in the rock. The distribution of karst areas in the U.S. is shown in Figure 10-3.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-7a, printed p. 241.

sections.title: Performance issues
sections.body: [p. 241] Performance issues. Karst features (such as caves, sinkholes, and open fractures) cause severe damage for engineering structures worldwide. Major problems encountered by engineers in karst terrain include collapse of subsurface voids, subsidence of soil cover into rock voids or sinkholes, and excavation difficulties over pinnacled bedrock. In karst terrain, the potential for unsatisfactory performance cannot be eliminated. Karst can suddenly manifest at the surface when site development activities result in overburden removal, additional surface water infiltration, or more severe groundwater fluctuations.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-7b, printed p. 241.

sections.title: Mitigation techniques
sections.body:
[p. 241] Mitigation techniques. Several mitigation techniques have been used in karst terrain for shallow foundations. Subsurface grouting is a common technique; however, is difficult to verify and could disrupt groundwater flow. Other mitigation techniques have included structure relocation, using mat or grid foundations, grade raise by fill placement, inverted rock filters or plugs where shallow rock exists, and surface water management. In karst terrain, additional borings, rock coring, and geophysical surveys may be warranted to better characterize soil and bedrock conditions.

[p. 242] Figure 10-3. Distribution of karst areas in relation to carbonate and sulfate rocks in the U.S. (from USGS 2020)

sections.title: Frozen ground
sections.body: [p. 242] Frozen ground is defined as soil or rock having a temperature below 32 °F, regardless of water or ice content. How deeply and quickly the ground freezes depends on many other factors. In most cases, the ground temperature can be quite different from the air temperature. Permafrost, or perennially frozen ground, is defined as soil or rock having temperatures below 32 °F during at least two consecutive winters and the intervening summer (Brown and Kupsch 1974). Detailed requirements of engineering design in frozen ground areas are provided in UFC series, Arctic and Subarctic Construction (UFC 3-130-01 through UFC 3-130-07).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-8, printed p. 242.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.body: [p. 242] Characteristics. Frozen soil generally consists of four components: soil particles, ice, water, and voids, and can be described using the methods outlined in ASTM D4083 and ASTM D7099. The voids are filled with ice, unfrozen water, and air. Ice may be distributed evenly, or it may have accumulated in the form of irregular or stratified ice inclusions. The engineering properties of frozen soil is complex and can range from brittle to plastic, depending on the volume of ice, ground temperature, water content, and saline content. For the purposes of this manual, areas of significant frost penetration may be defined as those in which freezing temperatures occur in the ground to sufficient depth to be a significant factor in foundation design. Areas of significant frost penetration may be subdivided as follows:
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-8a, printed p. 242.

sections.title: Seasonal frost areas
sections.body: [p. 243] Seasonal frost areas. Significant ground freezing occurs in these areas during the winter season, but without development of permafrost. In northern Texas, significant seasonal frost typically occurs about once every 10 years. A little farther north, it occurs every year. Depth of seasonal freezing increases northward with decreasing mean annual and winter air temperatures until permafrost is encountered. With still further decrease of air temperatures, the depth of annual freezing and thawing becomes progressively thinner (especially when the ground is more permanently frozen).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-8a(1), printed p. 243.

sections.title: Permafrost areas
sections.body: [p. 243] Permafrost areas. In these areas, perennially frozen ground is found below the annual frost zone. In North America, permafrost is found principally north of latitudes 55 to 65 degrees, although patches of permafrost are found much farther south on mountains where the temperature conditions are sufficiently low, including some mountains in the contiguous 48 States.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-8a(2), printed p. 243.

sections.title: Permafrost distribution
sections.body:
[p. 243] Permafrost distribution. The geographic boundaries between zones of continuous permafrost, discontinuous permafrost, and seasonal frost without permafrost are poorly defined, but are represented approximately in Figure 10-4.

sections.title: Seasonal frost areas
sections.body: [p. 244] Seasonal frost areas. Design of foundations in areas of seasonal frost where the material below the frost line remains unfrozen presents certain problems. In the spring, thaw and settlement of frost-heaved material in the annual frost zone could occur differentially, and a very wet, condition with temporary but substantial loss of shear strength can occur.

Note. Progressive freezing and frost heave of foundations can also develop under refrigerated warehouses and other facilities where sustained interior below-freezing temperatures are maintained.

sections.title: In permafrost areas, heat flow from buildings is a fundamental consideration
sections.body: [p. 244] In permafrost areas, heat flow from buildings is a fundamental consideration. Change from natural conditions that results in warming of the ground beneath a structure can result in progressive thawing of the permafrost layer over time (typically years) that is known as degradation. If the permafrost contains ice in excess of the natural void or fissure space of the material when unfrozen, progressive downward thaw may result in extreme settlements of overlying soil and structures.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-8b(3)(a), printed p. 244. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: This condition can be very serious because such subsidence is almost invariably …
sections.body: [p. 244] This condition can be very serious because such subsidence is almost invariably differential, and hence, very damaging to a structure. Degradation can occur not only from building heat but also from solar heating, as under pavements, from surface water and groundwater flow, and from underground utility lines. Proper insulation can prevent degradation in some situations, but where a continuous source of heat is also available, thaw can eventually occur.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-8b(3)(b), printed p. 244. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.body: [p. 245] Mitigation techniques.

sections.title: Seasonal frost areas
sections.body: [p. 245] Seasonal frost areas. For seasonal frost areas, foundation installation may be aided by ground thaw devices and designed using measures to protect against seasonal frost heave. Criteria for seasonal frost areas is provided in the UFC 3-130-04 and UFC 3-301-01. Design and construction standards can be found in ASCE 32.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-8c(1), printed p. 245.

sections.title: Permafrost regions
sections.body: [p. 245] Permafrost regions. Detailed requirements of engineering design in frozen ground areas, to include mitigation techniques, is provided in UFC 3-130-04. When constructing shallow foundations in permafrost regions, passive or active techniques are used to protect structures from permafrost degradation. Passive methods maintain the frozen state of the soil and could include using insulation, ventilation, or refrigeration systems such as thermosyphons. Active methods include removing and pre-thawing frozen soils that may be suitable for foundation stabilization.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-8c(2), printed p. 245.

sections.title: Scour and erosion
sections.body: [p. 245] Scour and erosion are the localized loss of soil around a foundation due to flowing water. Shallow foundations most affected by scour and erosion are usually located in or near water bodies (such as rivers, beaches) or areas of flash flooding.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-9, printed p. 245.

sections.title: Characterization
sections.body: [p. 245] Characterization. Scour effects may be localized or result in the complete undermining of a building foundation. Scour effects typically result from flooding or storm surge type events.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-9a, printed p. 245.

sections.title: Performance issues
sections.body: [p. 245] Performance issues. Excessive removal of the material around a shallow foundation or undermining of a footing can cause excessive deformation or structure collapse.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-9b, printed p. 245.

sections.title: Mitigation techniques
sections.body: [p. 245] Mitigation techniques. Scour and erosion countermeasures (such as structural features, river training, riprap, vegetation, geosynthetics) should be implemented for the design flood and the foundation constructed at sufficient depth beneath the maximum scour depth to provide sufficient bearing capacity and overall stability.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 10 (Problematic Ground Conditions), paragraph 10-9c, printed p. 245.
